title: food as practice
hook: a proud student is told to stop eating, and his father's lesson arrives as an ember

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice and a knock at the door: make much food, and turn no one away.

A student comes home after years of study, sure of himself, full of verses. You met him back in year three, the proud one: Shvetaketu. His father, Uddalaka, decides to test him, and the test isn't a debate. It's a diet. Eat nothing for a while, the father says. Drink all the water you like. Then come back and recite what you know. The experiment sits in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. Today, what a meal has to do with a mind.
screen: `A STUDENT HOME, SURE OF HIMSELF.` → `THE TEST IS A DIET.` → `WHAT A MEAL HAS TO DO WITH A MIND.`

segments.voice: It starts with a claim, paraphrased. Food, once eaten, divides three ways. The coarsest part leaves the body. The middle part becomes flesh. The finest part becomes mind. Uddalaka puts it in one line, in Sanskrit annamayam hi somya manah: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Water, he adds, becomes breath, and heat becomes speech. Then the test. The text says fifteen days without food, with water allowed. Shvetaketu comes back, and his father asks for the verses. They don't come to me, sir, he says. So Uddalaka gives him a picture. A great fire has burned down to one ember, the size of a firefly. It can't burn much now. Add straw, and it blazes again. Go and eat. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and the verses are all there. And he understood, the text says. Three things. First, it's humbling. The young scholar who thought learning lived somewhere above the body finds it leaning on lunch. Second, it's kind to the body. Nobody is scolded for needing to eat; the plate is part of how a person thinks. Third, it's a doorway. In this same chapter Uddalaka will say tat tvam asi, that thou art. He's teaching his son what a self is, and food is one of the first things he reaches for. And plainly, since these days hold Ayurveda to a careful standard: this is a teaching story, not a fasting plan, and nobody should copy the experiment. What it offers is a way to see a meal: not fuel poured in while the real you is somewhere else, but an ember being fed.
screen: `FOOD DIVIDES THREE WAYS` · `THE MIND, MY DEAR, IS MADE OF FOOD` · `AN EMBER THE SIZE OF A FIREFLY` · `A TEACHING STORY, NOT A FASTING PLAN`

segments.voice: Rest a hand low on the belly if you like, and let a small ember come to mind, glowing, about the size of a firefly. With each breath in let it brighten a little, the way a coal brightens when air reaches it, and with each breath out let it settle and glow. If you pray, give thanks for the food that is holding you up right now.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya, the finest part of a meal becomes mind, and a hungry student's verses come back after he eats. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. The mind, my dear, is made of food. Rest well.

howItsDone: Some Hindus fast on particular days as a devotional practice, while teachers of the Upanishads read Uddalaka's experiment as a lesson about the self, not as a fasting rule.
